title: Making a case
cando: argue for a position with evidence, and answer objections

about.text: In this lesson, you learn to argue for what you believe and to answer the other side fairly. You listen to a team debating whether to keep flexitime, read a group's response to a plan to close a library, and write your own response to a proposal. Then you take part in a structured debate in the live class.
goals: Make a case with a claim, a reason and evidence: The main reason is…, The evidence suggests…
Ask for evidence, and answer objections politely: Can you back that up? That may be true, but…
Concede a point, then counter it: admittedly, even so, on the other hand.
Read a consultation response and write your own response to a proposal.
Take part in a structured debate.

chapters.title: A debate at work
chapters.text:
This lesson is about making a case: arguing for what you believe, and answering the other side fairly.
We start at a team meeting. The team has tried flexitime for three months, and now they must decide whether to keep it.
Carlos is for it. Mei has an objection. Priya, the manager, has to decide.
Listen to how they disagree without getting angry. Carlos says: The main reason is that people are happier. Mei answers: That may be true, but three months isn't very long.
Then listen for the moment when Mei says: OK, I'll concede that. She accepts one point, and moves on to a stronger one.
You also learn words for a debate. A drawback is a disadvantage. If the benefits outweigh a drawback, they matter more. And to back something up is to give evidence for it.

chapters.title: Claim, reason, evidence
chapters.text:
The grammar has two parts.
The first is the shape of a good argument. A claim says what you think: we should keep flexitime. A reason says why: the main reason is that people get more done. Evidence is a fact that others can check: sick days fell by a third.
Be careful here. Say: the main reason is that. Don't say: the main reason is because.
The second part is conceding. Admittedly accepts a point for the other side. Admittedly, the trial was short. Even so gives your view again. Even so, the results were clear. On the other hand gives a different side.
Conceding one real point makes the rest of your case stronger, not weaker.

chapters.title: Having your say
chapters.text:
Next, you read a response to a consultation. The council wants to close a small library, and it has asked local people for their views.
A group of residents writes back. Notice how they do it. First, they accept what is true: the council must save money. Then they say where they disagree. Then they give evidence: numbers, not just feelings. And they finish with a proposal, not a threat.
Words like acknowledge, reconsider and in principle help you to sound firm, but polite.
Then you write your own response to a proposal. It can be a real one from your area or your work, or you can invent it.

chapters.title: The debate
chapters.text:
The task is a real debate in the live class. The topic is working from home two days a week.
You are in a team, for or against. First, give your case: a claim, a reason and evidence.
Then the other team answers, and here is the key skill. Don't just repeat yourself. Concede one point, clearly, and then counter it. For example: That may be true, and I'll concede that new staff need support. Even so, the evidence suggests that the team works well.
Don't concede something small that nobody cares about. Concede the other side's best point, and then show why your case is still stronger.
At the end, the class votes.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer text in which someone makes a case.
As you read, look for the claim, the reasons and the evidence. Does the writer answer the other side, or ignore it? Is the evidence something you could check, or only a feeling?
Then talk or write about it. Who do you agree with, and why?

warmup.prompt: Your manager wants to change how your team works, and you don't agree. What do you usually do?
choices: talk to the manager alone afterwards
say nothing and go along with it
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. It depends on you and on your workplace. In this lesson, you practise saying what you think clearly and calmly, with reasons.

conversation.title: Should we keep flexitime?
conversation.setting: The customer service team at Halden Insurance has tried flexitime for three months. Before the trial ends, Priya, the team manager, holds a short debate with Carlos and Mei.
lines: Priya
Right. The flexitime trial ends on Friday, so we need to decide. Carlos, you're in favour of keeping it?
Carlos
Yes, definitely. The main reason is that people are happier, and they get more done. The evidence suggests it's working: sick days fell by a third during the trial.
Mei
That may be true, but three months isn't very long. Sick days always fall in the summer.
Carlos
They do, but they fell compared with last summer too, not just compared with the spring.
Mei
OK, I'll concede that. My objection is different. Between eight and nine, there are often only two of us on the phones.
Priya
Can you back that up? I haven't seen any complaints.
Mei
Yes. Waiting times before nine went up from two minutes to six. Customers don't complain to us. They just hang up.
Carlos
Admittedly, that's a drawback. Even so, I think the benefits outweigh it. We could simply agree that three people always start at eight.
Mei
I wouldn't oppose that. I'm not against flexitime. I'm against empty phones.
Priya
So it sounds like a short-term problem with a simple fix, rather than a reason to stop.
Mei
In the short term, yes. But in the long term, we'll need better figures to justify it. I'd like to see them again in six months.
Priya
That's fair. Let's keep flexitime, with a rota for the early hour, and look at the figures again in March.

questions.q: What evidence does Carlos give for keeping flexitime?
questions.a: Sick days fell by a third.
questions.why: Carlos says: sick days fell by a third during the trial.

questions.a: Too few people answer the phones early in the morning.
questions.why: Mei says there are often only two people on the phones between eight and nine.

questions.a: to keep flexitime, with a rota for the early hour
wrong: to ask customers what they think
questions.why: Priya says: Let's keep flexitime, with a rota for the early hour.

phrases.use: Saying what the facts show, without claiming too much.
Admitting that the other side is right about one thing.
Saying exactly what you disagree with.

phrases.text: I think the benefits outweigh it.
phrases.use: Saying the good points matter more than a problem.
Making clear exactly what you oppose.

items.meaning: A discussion in which people give different opinions on a subject, sometimes with rules about who speaks when.
items.example: There was a lively debate about the new rota.

items.meaning: The arguments that support something, and the arguments that oppose it.
items.example: Let's list the arguments for and against before we decide.

items.meaning: A disadvantage or problem that makes something less good.
items.example: The main drawback of the flat is the noise.

items.meaning: To be more important than something else.
items.example: The benefits of the new system outweigh the costs.

items.meaning: To give good reasons for a decision or an action.
items.example: How can they justify such a big price rise?

items.meaning: To support a claim with facts or evidence.
items.example: Can you back up that figure?

items.meaning: Facts or documents that show that something is definitely true.
items.example: Keep your receipt as proof of purchase.

items.meaning: To question whether something is true or right.
items.example: Nobody challenged the manager's figures.

items.meaning: To disagree with a plan or an idea, and try to stop it.
items.example: Many residents oppose the new car park.

items.meaning: A reason you give for not agreeing with a plan or an idea.
items.example: Does anyone have any objections to the new timetable?

items.meaning: To admit, often unwillingly, that the other side is right about something.
items.example: I concede that the trial was short.

items.meaning: A short period when you test something new to see if it works.
items.example: The shop is staying open late on Thursdays as a trial.

items.meaning: A system that lets workers choose, within limits, when they start and finish work.
items.example: With flexitime, I can start at seven and leave at three.

items.meaning: Lasting, or having an effect, for a long time into the future.
items.example: We need a long-term plan, not a quick fix.

items.meaning: Lasting, or having an effect, for only a short time.
items.example: The loan was only a short-term solution.

sound.title: Where the stress falls: drawback, outweigh, back up
sound.explain: Many of this lesson's words have two parts, and one part is stronger. In nouns like drawback and flexitime, the first part is strong: DRAW-back, FLEXI-time. In the verb outweigh, and in phrasal verbs like back up, the second part is strong: out-WEIGH, back UP. Listen, then say each group.
lines: The main drawback is the early hour.
Can you back that up?
I think the benefits outweigh it.

sayIt.instructions: Say Carlos's and Mei's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Do you sound calm and sure, not angry?
lines: Yes, definitely. The main reason is that people are happier, and they get more done. The evidence suggests it's working: sick days fell by a third during the trial.
That may be true, but three months isn't very long. Sick days always fall in the summer.
OK, I'll concede that. My objection is different. Between eight and nine, there are often only two of us on the phones.
Admittedly, that's a drawback. Even so, I think the benefits outweigh it. We could simply agree that three people always start at eight.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Carlos makes a case, and Mei answers it. Some sentences give a reason or evidence. Others accept a point before they disagree.
examples: The main reason is that people are happier, and they get more done.
The evidence suggests it's working: sick days fell by a third during the trial.
That may be true, but three months isn't very long.
Admittedly, that's a drawback. Even so, I think the benefits outweigh it.
spot.question: Which sentence gives a reason? Which gives evidence that you could check? Which two accept a point from the other side, and then disagree?
spot.answer: The first gives Carlos's main reason for keeping flexitime: ‘The main reason is that…’. The second gives evidence, a fact anyone can check: sick days fell by a third. The last two accept a point first, with ‘That may be true’ and ‘Admittedly’, then disagree with ‘but’ and ‘Even so’.

rules.title: Making a case: claim, reason, evidence
rule: Claim: say what you think. We should keep flexitime.
Reason: say why. The main reason is that people get more done.
Evidence: back it up. The evidence suggests that… For example, …
Evidence is something others can check: figures, dates, what happened.
To ask for evidence, say: Can you back that up?
rules.mistake: Not: The main reason is because people are happier. Say: The main reason is that people are happier.

rules.title: Conceding: admittedly, even so, on the other hand
rule: Admittedly, + a point for the other side: Admittedly, the trial was short.
Even so, + your view again: Even so, the results were clear.
On the other hand, + a different side: On the other hand, the phones are busy at eight.
When you speak: That may be true, but … or OK, I'll concede that.
Concede something real, then counter it. It makes your case harder to dismiss.
rules.mistake: Not: Admittedly the trial was short, even so it worked. Say: Admittedly, the trial was short. Even so, it worked.

practice.q: The main reason is ___ staff get more done.
practice.why: The main reason is that + a sentence.

practice.q: ___, the trial was short. Even so, the results were good.
practice.why: Admittedly concedes a point for the other side.

practice.q: The trial was short. ___, the results were clear.
practice.why: Even so starts a new sentence and gives your view again after a concession.

practice.q: Flexitime helps people with long journeys. On the ___ hand, it can leave the phones empty early.
practice.why: On the other hand gives a different side of the argument.

practice.q: The evidence ___ that the change is working.
practice.why: The evidence is singular, so it suggests.

options: Sick days fell by a third.
I think we should keep it.
practice.a: Sick days fell by a third.
practice.why: Evidence is a fact that others can check.

practice.q: That may be true, ___ three months isn't very long.
practice.why: Only but can join the two parts with a comma.

practice.q: I ___ that the trial was short, but the results are clear.
practice.why: To concede is to admit that the other side is right about one point.

practice.q: Many staff ___ the plan. They say it would make their journeys longer.
practice.why: To oppose a plan is to disagree with it and try to stop it.

practice.q: Can you ___ that up with any figures?
practice.why: You back up a claim when you support it with evidence.

yourTurn.prompt: Your workplace or college wants to make a change: a ban on phones in meetings, an earlier start time, or an open-plan office. Write a short case of four or five sentences, for or against it. Give your claim, a reason and evidence. Then concede one point and counter it.
yourTurn.model: I think we should keep phones out of meetings. The main reason is that meetings finish faster when nobody is checking messages. The evidence suggests this works: since our team tried it in May, the Monday meeting has gone from an hour to forty minutes. Admittedly, people sometimes need to take an urgent call. Even so, they can step outside for a minute, so the rule still works.

text.title: Hartley Road Library: our response
text.body:
PRACTICE: this council and this library are not real.

NORTHBRIDGE COUNCIL · PUBLIC CONSULTATION
Proposal: to close Hartley Road Library and move its services to the Central Library
Response from the Friends of Hartley Road Library, a group of local residents · 14 October

1. What we accept
We acknowledge that the council must save £2 million this year, and that Hartley Road is the smallest of the town's four libraries. We also accept, in principle, that some services can move online.

2. Where we disagree
The proposal treats the library as a place to borrow books. That is only part of what it does. It is also the only public facility in Eastfield with free computers, and one of the few warm, quiet places where people can study or look for work.

3. Our case
Visits have risen by 20% in two years, and most of the people who use the computers are over 65 or out of work. Many of them do not have a car, and the Central Library is two buses away. The evidence suggests that closure would not move these people to another library: it would simply stop them using one. A petition against the closure has been signed by 1,200 residents.

4. The cost
The council says the building needs substantial investment: about £400,000 for a new roof. We do not challenge this figure. However, it does not take into account the money the library saves other services, for example by helping people to apply for jobs and benefits online.

5. What we propose
We ask the council to reconsider. The health centre next door is looking for more rooms, and sharing the building would help to fund the repairs. Our members would also be happy to volunteer, so that the library can stay open on Saturdays.

We would welcome a meeting to discuss these ideas before any decision is made.

gist.q: What is the main aim of this response?
gist.a: to persuade the council not to close the library
wrong: to complain about the library's opening hours
to ask for a bigger Central Library
gist.why: The group makes a case against the closure and asks the council to reconsider.

gist.q: What does the group agree with?
gist.a: The council needs to save money.
wrong: The roof does not need repairs.
gist.why: In section 1, they acknowledge that the council must save £2 million this year.

detail.q: How many residents have signed the petition?
detail.why: A petition against the closure has been signed by 1,200 residents.

detail.q: Why would the closure stop some people using a library at all?
detail.a: Many have no car, and the Central Library is two buses away.
wrong: The Central Library has no computers.
The Central Library is closed on Saturdays.
detail.why: Section 3 says many users do not have a car, and the Central Library is two buses away.

detail.q: What does the group say the council's cost figure leaves out?
detail.a: the money the library saves other services
wrong: the cost of a new roof
detail.why: The figure does not take into account the money the library saves other services.

detail.q: How could the repairs be paid for, according to the group?
detail.a: by sharing the building with the health centre
wrong: by charging people to use the computers
by closing the library on Saturdays
detail.why: Sharing the building with the health centre would help to fund the repairs.

items.meaning: A process in which an organisation, such as a council, asks the public for their views before it decides something.
items.example: The council has opened a consultation on the new parking rules.

items.meaning: A written request, signed by many people, asking someone in power to do or change something.
items.example: Over 3,000 people signed the petition to save the pool.

items.meaning: The permanent closing of a building, a service or a business.
items.example: The closure of the factory hit the town hard.

items.meaning: A building or a service provided for a particular purpose, such as a sports centre or a library.
items.example: The new health centre is a great facility for the area.

items.meaning: Money spent on something to make it better or more successful in the future.
items.example: The station needs serious investment.

items.meaning: To provide the money to pay for something.
items.example: The new bus route is funded by the council.

items.meaning: Large in amount or importance.
items.example: Repairing the bridge will cost a substantial amount of money.

items.meaning: To accept or admit that something is true.
items.example: The company acknowledged that mistakes had been made.

items.meaning: To think again about a decision, and possibly change it.
items.example: Please reconsider your decision to close the branch.

items.meaning: To think about something when you make a decision or a judgement.
items.example: The report doesn't take into account the cost of staff.

items.meaning: As a general idea, even if you don't yet agree with every detail.
items.example: We agree in principle, but we need to see the figures.

model.title: A response to a proposal
model.body:
Response to the proposal to end the Number 8 bus after 10 p.m.
From: Ana Costa, Eastfield resident
I acknowledge that the late buses carry fewer passengers than daytime ones, and I accept in principle that the council needs to save money.
However, I oppose the proposal as it stands. Many people who use the late bus are shift workers at the hospital and the warehouses, and they have no other way to get home. The evidence suggests that they are not a small group: on my own bus last Tuesday, there were fourteen passengers after ten o'clock.
Admittedly, fourteen people do not fill a bus. Even so, cutting the service would cost these workers far more than it would save the council.
I would ask the council to reconsider, and to take into account a cheaper option: a smaller bus after 10 p.m., instead of no bus at all.

write.task: Write your own response to a proposal, real or invented: closing a local facility, changing a service, or building something new near your home or work. Write 150 to 200 words in four parts: what you accept, where you disagree, your evidence, and what you propose.
checklist: I accepted at least one point from the other side.
I gave a clear reason and at least one piece of evidence.
I used admittedly, even so or on the other hand, with the right punctuation.
I ended with a clear, polite proposal.

card.title: The debate
card.situation: Your class is a company's staff meeting. The motion is: Everyone should be able to work from home two days a week. The class splits into two teams, for and against.
card.goal: Argue your side with a claim, a reason and evidence. When the other team answers, concede one point clearly, then counter it.

prepare.notes: Write your claim in one sentence. Then write your best reason, one piece of evidence, the strongest objection the other team will make, and your answer to it.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher chairs the debate. Each team gives its case in two minutes. Then each speaker answers one point from the other team: concede it, then counter it. At the end, the class votes.
doIt.wehel: Let's have a short debate. The topic is: Everyone should be able to work from home two days a week. I am for it, and you are against it. Give me one strong objection at a time. After each of my answers, tell me if I conceded a point and then countered it. Use clear, simple English.

model.title: Working from home: the debate
lines: Chair
The motion is: everyone should be able to work from home two days a week. You're for it. Please start.
You
Thank you. I think this change would help both the staff and the company. The main reason is that people lose too much time travelling. Most of us spend over an hour a day on trains and buses.
Chair
Thank you. Omar, you're against the motion.
Omar
I oppose it. The main reason is that teams need to be together. New staff learn by watching others and asking questions.
You

That may be true, and I'll concede that new staff need more support. Even so, the evidence suggests that two days at home don't harm a team. When our sales team tried it last year, their results actually improved.
Omar
Can you back that up? One team for a few months isn't proof.
You
It isn't proof, I agree. But it's better evidence than a guess. And new staff could come in every day for their first three months.
Omar
That answers part of my objection. On the other hand, some people don't have a quiet place to work at home.
You
True, and that's why it should be a choice, not a rule. Anyone who prefers the office can keep coming in.
Chair
Thank you both. Let's hear from the rest of the class before we vote.
compare: Did you give a claim, a reason and evidence?
Did you concede one point clearly, with That may be true, Admittedly or I'll concede that?
After conceding, did you counter it with Even so, But or On the other hand?
Did you stay calm and polite, even when you disagreed?

canDo: I can argue for a position with a claim, a reason and evidence.
I can ask for evidence and answer objections politely.
I can concede a point, then counter it with even so or on the other hand.
I can read a consultation response and write my own response to a proposal.
I can take part in a structured debate.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. Who is trying to persuade whom, and what about?
reading.talk: Who made the strongest case in the text? Did they give evidence, and did they answer the other side fairly? Write three or four sentences, or discuss it with Wehel.

quiz.q: A disadvantage is also called a ___ .
quiz.why: A drawback is a disadvantage or problem.

quiz.q: The benefits ___ the costs, so we should go ahead.
quiz.why: outweigh: to be more important than something else.

quiz.q: Admittedly, it's expensive. ___, I think it's worth it.
quiz.why: Even so gives your view again after a concession.

options: I'll admit the trial was short.
quiz.a: I'll admit the trial was short.
quiz.why: To concede is to admit that the other side is right about something.

quiz.q: When a council asks the public for their views before it decides, it holds a ___ .
quiz.why: A consultation asks the public for their views.

quiz.q: The council should take ___ account the views of local people.
quiz.why: take into account: think about something when you decide.

quiz.q: Many residents ___ the plan to close the pool.
quiz.why: You oppose a plan, but you object to it.

quiz.q: Sales rose ___ 20%, from 500 to 600 a month.
quiz.why: rose by + the size of the change.

quiz.q: Litter attracts rats, which ___ turn keeps people away.
quiz.why: which in turn: the effect becomes the next cause.

quiz.q: The old system was slow. ___, it was cheap.
quiz.why: However starts a new sentence, with a comma after it.

liveClass: Day 1: run the flexitime meeting in groups of three, then again with a different change: an open-plan office, or a later start. Every objection must be answered with That may be true, but… or I'll concede that.
Day 2: the task. Chair a structured debate on working from home: two teams, two-minute cases, then each speaker concedes one point and counters it. The class votes at the end.
Day 3: talk about the book: who made the strongest case, and did they answer the other side? Then two learners read their consultation responses aloud, and the class finds the concession in each.
